notes:
I found no material from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), from Orthodox sources (oca.org), or from sites describing prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so those are left out. Most of the denominational views below come from older commentators collected on biblehub, studylight and blueletterbible. On this psalm the traditions mostly agree; there are only a few real disagreements, and I flag them.

**Overview / setting**
- Adam Clarke (Methodist) links the psalm to Absalom's rebellion and calls it an evening hymn David's company sang before bed. This Psalm seems to have been composed on the same occasion with the preceding, viz., Absalom's rebellion. It appears to have been an evening hymn, sung by David and his company previously to their going to rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-4.html
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) disagrees. He thinks the Absalom link is probably incorrect because the psalm is about David's reputation being slandered, not his physical safety. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- The NET notes summarise the psalm this way: the psalmist asks God to hear his prayer, expresses his confidence that the Lord will intervene, and urges his enemies to change their ways and place their trust in God. He concludes with another prayer for divine intervention and again affirms his absolute confidence in God's protection. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+4%3A1-3

**v. 1**
- Traditional reading: David uses God's past help as grounds for asking again. Spurgeon calls this another instance of David's common habit of pleading past mercies as a ground for present favour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps004.cfm
- "Relieved" literally means "made room." Precept Austin explains: Distress (tsar) pictures narrowness or being hemmed in. David is essentially saying, "When I was squeezed into a tight place, You made room for me." https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-4-commentary
- Clarke says David asks for help as pure mercy: I shall always need thy help; I shall never deserve to have it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/psalms/4-1.html
- **Where traditions differ: "God of my righteousness."**
  - *God who makes me righteous.* Gill (Baptist) allows this reading: God was the author of his righteousness, and was the justifier of him, by imputing the righteousness of his Son unto him. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/mcb/psalms/4-1.html Guzik reads it similarly: David knew that his righteousness came from God, and not from himself. He calls upon the God who makes him righteous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
  - *God who defends my just cause.* Barnes (Presbyterian) says David's plea is not on the ground of his own claim as a righteous man, but it is that, in this particular case, he was wrongfully persecuted. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly rejects the imputation reading: Not "the God who imputes to me righteousness," as some render, but "the God who sees that I and my cause are righteous". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-1.htm
  - *Both together.* Spurgeon combines the views: God is the author, the witness, the maintainer, the judge, and the rewarder of my righteousness. Keil and Delitzsch call God both the author of righteousness, and the vindicator of misjudged and persecuted righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-1.htm
- Modern scholarship: the NET translates "O God who vindicates me." It also notes that the Hebrew verb tense behind "relieved" is uncertain. The translation above assumes that the psalmist is expressing his certitude and confidence that God will intervene. The psalmist is so confident of God's positive response to his prayer, he can describe God's deliverance as if it had already happened. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4
- Catholic (Augustine): Augustine's Latin text reads the line as past tense, "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me." He explains the enlargement as being led from the straits of sadness into the broad ways of joy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm

**v. 2**
- Barnes takes "my honor" to mean David's rank. If the setting is Absalom, the enemies were trying to take his crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-4.html
- Clarke says the Hebrew phrase points to leading men, Not plebeians, but nobles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-4.html
- Thomas Watson, quoted by Spurgeon, on "love vanity": They that love sin, love vanity; they chase a bubble, they lean upon a reed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps004.cfm
- Modern scholarship: some think "vanity" and "lies" mean idols. The NET says there is no solid immediate contextual evidence for such an interpretation. It is more likely that the psalmist addresses those who threaten him (see v. 1) and refers in a general way to their sinful lifestyle. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+4%3A1-3
- Augustine reads the verse as a call to stop seeking happiness in low things: Truth alone, from which all things are true, makes blessed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry gives this as a reason the enemies should not persecute the godly man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_004.cfm
- Reformed/Calvinist emphasis: Spurgeon (Baptist, Calvinist) reads it as teaching election: the fact that the godly are the chosen of God, and are, by distinguishing grace, set apart and separated from among men. His sermon outline for the verse is headed "Election." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps004.cfm
- Guzik focuses on practice. He lists reasons prayers may go unanswered, such as unconfessed sin and not abiding in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- Modern scholarship: the NET says this is a general principle, though the singular form and the parallel line indicate he has himself in mind as the representative godly person. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa+4%3A1-3
- Augustine's Latin reads "the Lord has magnified his Holy One," and he applies it to Christ, whom He raised up from below, and placed in heaven at His right hand. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm

**v. 4 (the main translation debate)**
- **"Tremble" or "be angry"?** The Hebrew word can mean either.
  - Calvin takes "tremble" as a call for the enemies to repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/4-4.html
  - Wesley (Methodist) has Be afraid, if not of me, yet of God, who hath engaged in my cause. His fellow Methodist Benson agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/4-4.html
  - Spurgeon: "Tremble and sin not." How many reverse this counsel and sin but tremble not. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-4.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek Septuagint's "Be ye angry, and sin not." Some scholars prefer it, and it may also seem to have the sanction of St. Paul in Ephesians 4:26. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-4.htm
  - Guzik (and the BSB) take "be angry." He applies it to David himself: he had reason to be angry but no reason to sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
  - Precept Austin also links the "trembling" to anger: In context it seems to be a righteous indignation directed against the sons of men who love what is worthless. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-4-commentary
- **Who is being spoken to?** Most older commentators (Barnes, Calvin, Wesley) say David is warning his enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/4-4.html Guzik instead puts verses 4–5 under the heading "David talks to himself." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- "Search your heart… be still": Matthew Henry says that after asking your conscience a question, you should be silent, and wait for an answer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_004.cfm Guzik contrasts biblical meditation, which fills the mind with God's word, with Eastern meditation, which tries to empty it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- Modern scholarship: the NET reads "be still" as possibly "wail/lament," that is, repent. It also gives "be quiet" as another option. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4
- Catholic: Augustine offers two readings. One is to let anger arise but not consent to it. The other is to be ye angry with yourselves for your past sins, and henceforth cease to sin. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm Aquinas cites a gloss on this verse saying "The movement of anger is not in our power." https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3158.htm

**v. 5**
- **What are the "sacrifices"?** Commentators differ.
  - The Geneva Bible notes (Reformed) say: Serve God purely, and not with outward ceremonies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-5.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist) says they mean a real sacrifice such as the law prescribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/4-5.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says animal sacrifices are scarcely meant; certainly not, if the time of the composition is that of David's exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-5.htm
  - Guzik sees value in religious practice, but says it can never replace trust in the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- Christ-centred applications: Spurgeon: O sinners, flee ye to the sacrifices of Calvary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/4-5.htm Clarke says no one can approach God except through the Mediator. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-4.html
- Modern scholarship: the NET translates "Offer the prescribed sacrifices." It reads "trust in the Lord" as David urging his enemies to make peace with God. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4
- Catholic: Augustine connects this with Psalm 51's "broken spirit." He takes the sacrifice to be repentance, or the righteous works that follow repentance. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry, using verse 7, says the "good" the many wanted was grain and wine, that is, worldly plenty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_004.cfm Guzik instead hears the voice of a discouraged cynic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/
- Both Spurgeon and Guzik connect "light of your face" to the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26. Spurgeon says it includes reconciliation, assurance, communion, benediction, in a word, the fulness of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps004.cfm
- Modern scholarship: the NET translates "Smile upon us." It says the idiom probably refers to a smile, which means favour and blessing. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4
- Catholic:
  - Augustine's Latin reads "the light of your countenance is stamped on us." He says it is stamped as a penny is stamped with the king's image. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801004.htm
  - John Paul II's *Veritatis Splendor* opens with this verse. He uses it to teach that the light of truth shining in the human spirit is how we tell good from evil. https://www.newadvent.org/library/docs_jp02vs.htm

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon: Christ in the heart is better than corn in the barn, or wine in the vat. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps004.cfm
- Barnes says "grain and wine" stand for worldly prosperity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-4.html
- The Biblical Illustrator mentions another reading: "from the time" their grain and wine increased. This would refer to the supplies David received as an exile at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 16–17). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/4-1.html
- Bible Hub's study notes link "grain and new wine" to harvest feasts such as Tabernacles. https://biblehub.com/psalms/4.htm
- Modern scholarship: the NET notes the verb could also be future: "you will make me happier." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4

**v. 8**
- Barnes: David is surrounded by danger but so confident in God that he will sleep calmly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-4.html
- Clarke: I am safe, because I enjoy the light of thy countenance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-4.html
- **What does "alone" go with?** Guzik cites G. Campbell Morgan, who takes "alone" to describe David, not God: David is safe "in seclusion" with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-4/ The NET similarly takes the word with "dwell" (God keeps enemies away), but gives "you alone, Lord" as an option. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=4
